source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
quote: the imagined 'editor' of Farmer Giles to criticise its imagined 'author'

verdict.trueWording: extremely unfair of the imagined 'editor'... to criticise its imagined 'author'
verdict.note: Quote verbatim, and the continuation is verbatim too: 'that "author", like Tolkien, "lived himself in the lands of the Little Kingdom" and knew what he was writing about.' The editor-over-author two-layer point is squarely Shippey's. What the page does not do is locate that apparatus in the Foreword or call it short; the word 'foreword' does not occur in the passage.

claim: Distances and directions in the tale map onto real Oxfordshire places (Ham/Thame, Tamworth, Farthingho, the Rollright Stones) at a parochial scale, so the Little Kingdom is measured like a real county.
source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
quote: proof of the 'Little Kingdom's' lack of territorial ambition

verdict.trueWording: Thame in Buckinghamshire; Farthingho in Northamptonshire; parochial scale
verdict.note: Quote verbatim. Shippey gives Ham = now Thame, twelve miles east of Oxford; the Middle Kingdom's capital 'sounds like Tamworth... sixty-eight miles from Thame'; Farthingho 'on a direct line... about a third of the way' as 'proof of the Little Kingdom's lack of territorial ambition'; Wales and the Pennines 'on this parochial scale suitably far off'; the Standing Stones = the Rollright Stones on the Warwickshire/Oxfordshire boundary. The counties Shippey actually names are Buckinghamshire, Northamptonshire and Warwickshire, not Oxfordshire.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'real Oxfordshire places' - Shippey puts Thame in Buckinghamshire, Farthingho in Northamptonshire, and Tamworth as the Mercian capital

claim: The tale's narrator was 'Daddy' in the oral original, became 'the family jester', and took on a formal scholarly tone when the story was enlarged by half for an academic essay club in 1938.
source: Hammond & Scull, 'Farmer Giles of Ham' (Tolkien Estate)

verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the narrator took on a formal scholarly tone at the 1938 enlargement — the page dates the mock-scholarly voice to the 1949 revision instead
verdict.trueWording: For this larger, more academic audience, he added many proper names, jokes, and allusions
verdict.note: Raw page fetched (200, live). Quote 'the family jester' is verbatim: 'In the second version of the story, the narrator is "the family jester"'. Supported: narrated by 'Daddy' in the first version; 'enlarging it by some fifty per cent' in January 1938 for the Lovelace Society, 'an undergraduate essay club at Oxford's Worcester College'. NOT supported: any narratorial shift to scholarly tone at that 1938 stage — the page says the 1938 additions were 'proper names, jokes, and allusions', and places the apparatus later: 'Tolkien again revised the text, and added a mock foreword' before the 1949 publication. Second minor slip: 'Daddy' narrates the first written version, not the oral original.

source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth

verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'a Latin binomial' — the page shows only the genus name, Tolkien's hedge 'a variety probably of Nicotiana', which is a uninomial, not a binomial

claim: The instinct of linguistic invention is the fitting of notion to oral symbol and pleasure in contemplating the relation — words must sound like what they mean.

quote: the fitting of notion to oral symbol

verdict.note: PDF downloaded from gwern (HTTP 200, 957,151 B, 26 pp — the 'A Secret Vice' text as printed in The Monsters and the Critics) and text-extracted with pdfminer. Quote verbatim: 'The instinct for “linguistic invention” - the fitting of notion to oral symbol, and pleasure in contemplating the new relation established, is rational, and not perverted.' Nowhere does the page prescribe that words must sound like what they mean; that limb is the claim's own gloss.

claim: An invented language with individual flavour must have a mythology woven into it, and conversely language construction will breed a mythology — names and tongue come first, the world grows to fit.
